Thanks for making time, Fabio. Let me be direct. Your pilot with Clearline looks interesting, but cross-border settlement is still a gray area for most regulators.
I understand. From our side, it seems that the technology is ready. What appears to be missing is a clear set of rules. Is that a fair reading?
That's fair. Regulators tend to move slowly when two countries are involved. Each side wants a full audit trail before it says yes.
That makes sense. So a regulatory sandbox is likely to be the safest first step for us?
Probably, yes. Inside a sandbox, you're still subject to the main rules, but some reporting obligations are lighter for twelve months.
Twelve months sounds reasonable. And what happens when the test ends? Is there likely to be a grace period?
Usually, yes, about six months, so you have time to comply with the full framework. But I can't promise anything. It depends on the results.
Of course. We'd rather err on the side of caution. We don't want to look like we're asking for special treatment.
Good. Then I'd suggest you read the new consultation paper first. It seems to answer most of your questions, and the comment period closes in May.

I've spent twenty years between banks and regulators, and I see the same mistake again and again. Bankers go into a meeting with a regulator as if it were a sales pitch. It isn't. A regulator is not a client. Their job is to protect the system, so they tend to listen for risk, not for opportunity. Three things help. First, don't overstate. If you say your solution is completely safe, they will stop trusting you. Say that it seems to work well in the tests, and show the data. Second, bring the audit trail. Regulators are likely to ask how every transaction can be checked later. And third, ask questions. Ask what worries them. A good meeting with a regulator feels less like a negotiation and more like a careful conversation between two people who both want the system to work.

Good morning, everyone. Before we open the floor, a short update on the cross-border sandbox. This year we received forty-two applications, and we accepted nine. Most of the projects that we rejected seemed to be ready technically, but they did not have a clear plan for data protection. So please, if you apply next year, start there. The next window opens on the first of March and closes at the end of April. Projects in the sandbox are subject to the same core rules as everyone else, but they report every quarter instead of every month. And one last point. It appears that many teams find our consultation paper too long. We hear you. A short summary is likely to be published next month.
